bib.title: Controllable Text Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey

read.skipped: Reference list (offset 137309 onward) skimmed only for arXiv ids; body, tables and conclusion read in full. The text has no appendices.

question: How can controllable text generation (CTG) for LLMs be defined, classified by task and by method, evaluated, and what challenges remain?
contributions: Exploration of Model Expression and CTG Quality
Innovative Task Classification Framework: content control (hard control) vs attribute control (soft control)
Systematic Classification of CTG Methods: training-stage methods and inference-stage methods

results.claim: CTG tasks split into content control (hard control: structure, vocabulary) and attribute control (soft control: safety, sentiment, style, topic).
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: Section 3 categorizes CTG tasks into content control (or linguistic control/hard control) and attribute control (or semantic control/soft control).

results.claim: CTG methods split by intervention stage into training-stage (retraining, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning) and inference-stage (prompt engineering, latent space manipulation, decoding-time intervention).
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: CTG methods are divided into two main stages: the training stage and the inference stage

results.claim: Prompt engineering controls output through the input only, needs no parameter change, and suits quick adjustment of generation strategy; its success depends on the model following the instruction.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: Because prompt engineering does not require altering model parameters, it is suitable for quickly adjusting generation strategies.

results.claim: Hard prompts are simple but may offer limited fine-grained control.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: However, they may offer limited fine-grained control.

results.claim: Hard prompts are highly sensitive to word choice; soft prompts (trainable vectors) are offered as the fix but cost interpretability and need initial tuning.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: Hard prompt is highly sensitive to word choice, where even minor changes can significantly impact generation quality.

results.claim: Prompt-based control only works as well as the model's instruction following; fine-tuning on curated data can raise responsiveness.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: If the model’s ability to follow prompt-encoded instructions is limited, the output may not align with expected results.

results.claim: Authors appeal for prompt baselines: prompts remain effective in many cases, so prompt-based methods should not be overlooked, and CTG papers should include prompt-based baselines.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: prompts remain effective in many cases, suggesting that prompt-based methods should not be overlooked.

results.claim: Strict lexical (hard) control is still unsatisfactory in existing models.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: in tasks requiring strict lexical control, model performance is often unsatisfactory [4].

results.claim: Decoding-time intervention is plug-and-play and flexible but adds inference time and can hurt fluency by forcing less likely tokens.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: This dependency can increase inference time due to the additional computation needed to adjust the output.

results.claim: Inference-stage methods need no retraining and give real-time control; training-stage methods need substantial data and compute and are less flexible.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: Inference phase methods do not require retraining and can dynamically adjust model outputs during generation, providing real-time control.

results.claim: Retraining is impractical for modern LLMs because of compute and data cost.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: These drawbacks make retraining methods less practical when dealing with modern LLMs.

results.claim: Fine-tuning is a balance between adaptability and resource use but depends on dataset quality.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: The quality of the dataset used for fine-tuning is crucial, as it directly affects the model’s ability to adapt to the desired control attributes.

results.claim: Control and helpfulness trade off: a refusal is safe but unhelpful; Safe RLHF balances them with separate reward and cost models.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: Separate reward and cost models are then trained to predict preferences for helpfulness and harmlessness.

results.claim: Spurious correlations in training data (for example positive sentiment co-occurring with science topics) degrade controllability.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: This phenomenon degrades the quality and controllability of the generated text and risks introducing bias and inaccuracies.

results.claim: PREADD controls an attribute by contrasting next-token log-probabilities with and without a prefix, scaled by a multiplier alpha.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors

results.claim: Latent space manipulation adds a guiding vector to layer activations; effect varies with architecture and task, so it is less predictable.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: making it less predictable and sometimes less reliable

results.claim: Evaluation uses automatic metrics (n-gram overlap, LM-based, distance-based, attribute classifiers/APIs), human evaluation (A/B, Likert) and LLM-based evaluation.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: Evaluation metrics for CTG tasks can be broadly categorized into three types: automatic evaluation, human evaluation, and LLM-based evaluation methods

results.claim: LLM-based evaluation is cheaper than human evaluation and reduces annotator subjective bias to some extent.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors
results.quote: LLM-based methods are more practical, significantly reducing evaluation costs

results.claim: Listed open challenges: reduced fluency and practicality, multi-attribute control, incomplete attribute decoupling, decoding time, imprecise content control.
results.setup: Survey statement, no experiment run by the authors

limits: Pure literature survey: no experiments, no comparative numbers across methods, so no claim here ranks one control method over another.
Reference cutoff is 2024; coverage of work after August 2024 is absent.

Prompt engineering gets short treatment (Sec 6.1, about two pages) and is framed around AutoPrompt, DAs, PCFG and soft-prompt tuning; instruction-following prompting of chat LLMs, system prompts, few-shot examples and structured-output modes are not covered as control methods.
The text cites Ashok and Poczos 2024 for the claim that prompts remain effective but reports none of its numbers.
Most surveyed methods target GPT-2-scale or T5-scale models; the survey itself does not say which carry over to current chat LLMs.
Authors concede decoding-stage methods face a time-versus-effect balance and that multi-attribute control is early stage.
practices: Choose the control method for the application scenario; effectiveness is the ultimate criterion (Sec 9.2.1).
Do not overlook prompt-based methods; they remain effective in many cases (Sec 9.2.1).
Use prompt-based techniques as baselines when comparing CTG methods so baselines are representative (Sec 9.2.3).
Prefer inference-stage methods when retraining is impractical or real-time adjustment is needed (Sec 5.4, 6.4).
Keep controlled output helpful: a bare refusal is not good control; give constructive guidance (Sec 1.1.2, Fig 8).
Check fluency alongside attribute accuracy; strong attribute control can damage fluency (Air-Decoding discussion, Sec 6.3.2).
Combine prompt engineering with fine-tuning on curated task data to raise responsiveness to prompts (Sec 6.1.2).
Evaluate control with attribute classifiers or APIs plus fluency and diversity metrics, supplemented by human or LLM judges (Sec 7).
Broaden test tasks beyond toxicity, emotion, topic and lexicon to style and form (Sec 9.2.2).

terms.definition: technologies that ensure generated text meets both high-quality standards and the specific needs of various applications; guides text generation to follow predefined control conditions, such as safety or sentiment, while maintaining quality like fluency and diversity
clearly defined instructions through human-computer interaction (e.g., input prompts)
ensuring that the generated text meets certain standards even when such requirements are not explicitly stated
focuses on specific elements of the generated text, such as its structure and vocabulary
focuses on abstract language attributes of the text, such as sentiment, style, and topic
training a new model from scratch or fundamentally modifying the architecture of an existing model to better accommodate specific control conditions
a pre-trained model is adjusted using a smaller, specific dataset to better align with particular control attributes without the need to train from scratch
discrete prompts expressed in natural language
continuous and trainable vectors embedded in the model's input space
adding guiding vectors to the activations in certain layers of LLMs; h_mod = h_orig + delta h
manipulating the logits or probability distribution of the model's output during decoding; p'(x_t|x_<t) = Adjust(p(x_t|x_<t), C)
irrelevant or coincidental features in the training data are mistakenly identified by the model as significant attributes
strong attribute control can impair fluency
